## Step 19: settle x4 and test a larger weight on x1

**What step 18 showed.** Moving x4 from −0.4 to −0.2 left the loss almost unchanged (0.4724 → 0.4723). The best value is somewhere between the two, so I fix x4 at −0.3.

**This step.** Raise x1 from 0.3 to 0.5. On its own x1 was one of the stronger positive features, so its weight may be set too low. Everything else stays as in step 18, apart from x4 at −0.3.

```python
import numpy as np
import math

def build_weights():
    # Linear logistic coefficients on standardised features
    w = np.zeros(13, dtype=np.float32)
    w[10] = 1.2    # dominant positive feature
    w[4]  = -0.3   # negative feature, mostly redundant (optimum ~-0.3)
    w[1]  = 0.5    # positive (testing stronger: was 0.3)
    w[5]  = 0.25   # positive
    w[9]  = 0.25   # positive
    w[2]  = 0.1    # weak positive
    w[0]  = -0.15  # weak negative (binary)
    w[3]  = -0.15  # weak negative, skewed tail
    w[8]  = -0.1   # weak negative

    b = -0.6       # bias for class-1 logit

    fc1_w = np.zeros((16, 13), dtype=np.float32)
    fc1_b = np.zeros(16, dtype=np.float32)
    fc1_w[0] = w        # h0 = relu(w.x)
    fc1_w[1] = -w       # h1 = relu(-w.x)

    fc2_w = np.zeros((2, 16), dtype=np.float32)
    fc2_b = np.zeros(2, dtype=np.float32)
    # class-1 logit = h0 - h1 + b = w.x + b ; class-0 logit = 0
    fc2_w[1, 0] = 1.0
    fc2_w[1, 1] = -1.0
    fc2_b[1] = b

    return {
        "fc1.weight": fc1_w,
        "fc1.bias": fc1_b,
        "fc2.weight": fc2_w,
        "fc2.bias": fc2_b,
    }
```
